title: Level 1 – Qualified Nurse
subtitle: Becoming a Professional Nurse
intro: Welcome to GNPS Program 9 - Professionalism in Nursing Practice. Professional nursing requires more than technical competence. Every action, conversation, record and decision reflects the nurse's accountability to patients, the profession and the wider community. This level is designed around the professional, ethical and legal capabilities expected within national nursing education programs and by nursing regulatory bodies across different countries. It develops the essential knowledge, attitudes and behaviours required to practise safely, protect patient rights and maintain public trust. Throughout this level you will strengthen your ability to: Explain the role and identity of the professional nurse Apply core ethical principles to routine nursing care Practise within scope, competence and organisational policy Protect privacy, confidentiality and dignity Support informed consent and the right to refuse treatment Document care accurately, objectively and promptly Communicate respectfully with patients, families and teams Use delegation principles safely Reflect on practice and maintain professional boundaries Patients depend on nurses not only for clinical care but also for honesty, advocacy, confidentiality and sound judgement. Small professional failures - an inaccurate record, an inappropriate disclosure or an unchallenged unsafe order - can cause serious harm. By the end of Level 1, you should be able to apply professional standards, ethical principles and basic legal responsibilities consistently within your scope of practice. Level 1 - Qualified Nurse

content.text: Professional identity is expressed through knowledge, conduct, communication and responsibility. Nurses are accountable for the decisions they make, the care they provide and the actions they delegate. Accountability also includes recognising limits and seeking help before patient safety is compromised.
Learning outcomes
Describe the roles of the professional nurse Explain accountability and responsibility
Recognise scope-of-practice limits Maintain appropriate professional boundaries
Professional Roles Nurses act as caregivers, advocates, educators, coordinators and collaborators. Each role requires respectful communication, sound judgement and attention to patient goals.

Accountability and Responsibility Responsibility refers to duties accepted within a role. Accountability means being answerable for decisions and outcomes. Following an instruction does not remove the duty to question an unsafe action.

Scope and Competence Scope is shaped by law, registration, education, competence and workplace policy. Nurses should not perform unfamiliar or unauthorised activities without appropriate preparation and supervision.

Professional Boundaries The therapeutic relationship exists to meet the patient's needs. Personal, financial, romantic or dual relationships can create exploitation, favouritism or loss of objectivity.

A newly qualified nurse is asked to manage an unfamiliar central-line procedure alone. Rather than pretending competence, the nurse explains the limitation, reviews the procedure and requests supervised practice. This protects the patient and demonstrates accountability.
Key learning points
Professionalism is shown through everyday behaviour Practise only within scope and competence
Question unsafe instructions respectfully Maintain clear therapeutic boundaries

Ethical principles help nurses reason through choices that affect dignity, safety and fairness. They are not abstract ideas; they guide consent, truth-telling, advocacy, privacy and decisions about treatment.
Learning outcomes
Explain major ethical principles Respect patient autonomy and informed choice
Protect dignity and fairness Recognise conflicts between ethical principles
Autonomy recognises the person's right to make informed decisions, including decisions that professionals may not prefer.
Beneficence and Nonmaleficence Beneficence means promoting good, while nonmaleficence means avoiding or minimising harm. Nurses often balance potential benefit against burden and risk.
Justice concerns fairness, equal respect and appropriate distribution of care and resources.
Fidelity and Veracity Fidelity means keeping professional commitments. Veracity requires honesty. False reassurance or hiding important information weakens trust.

A competent patient refuses a blood transfusion for deeply held beliefs. The nurse confirms that the patient understands the risks, communicates the decision to the team and advocates for alternative management. Respect for autonomy remains central.
Key learning points
Ethical principles support structured reasoning Respect informed decisions, including refusal
Honesty and fairness preserve trust Seek help when principles conflict

Legal and professional duties protect patients from unwanted treatment, privacy breaches and unsafe continuity of care. Informed consent, confidentiality and accurate records are core nursing responsibilities.
Learning outcomes
Explain the elements of informed consent Protect privacy and confidentiality
Document care objectively and promptly Recognise common legal risks
Informed Consent Valid consent requires capacity, adequate information and voluntariness. Nurses may witness consent or support understanding but should not provide explanations outside their role.
Right to Refuse A person with capacity may refuse treatment. The nurse should assess understanding, explore concerns, notify the appropriate clinician and document the discussion without coercion.

Privacy and Confidentiality Information should be accessed and shared only for legitimate care purposes. Conversations in public spaces, casual messaging and social-media posts can breach confidentiality.

Documentation Records should be timely, accurate, factual and attributable. They should show assessment, action, response and escalation. Documentation should never be altered deceptively or completed in advance.

A relative telephones asking for test results. The nurse cannot confirm the caller's authority and therefore explains that information cannot be disclosed. The nurse follows the organisation's process for authorised communication.
Key learning points
Consent must be informed and voluntary Share information only with appropriate authority
Document facts rather than opinions Never use social media to discuss patient care

Professional nursing depends on clear communication, safe teamwork and willingness to reflect. Delegation can improve care, but the nurse remains responsible for assessing whether the task, person and circumstances are appropriate.
Learning outcomes
Communicate assertively and respectfully Apply basic delegation principles
Manage disagreement professionally Use reflection to improve practice
Assertive Communication Assertive communication is clear, respectful and focused on patient safety. It differs from passive silence and aggressive blame.

Delegation Safe delegation considers the right task, circumstance, person, direction and supervision. Assessment, clinical judgement, teaching and evaluation generally remain with the registered nurse.
Conflict and Escalation Disagreement should be addressed through facts, patient needs and approved escalation pathways. Hierarchy should not prevent speaking up.
Reflective Practice Reflection examines what happened, why it happened and what could improve. It supports learning, resilience and continuing professional development.

A registered nurse delegates routine observations for a stable patient to an appropriately trained assistant, provides clear parameters and reviews the results. When the assistant reports a change, the nurse reassesses the patient immediately.
Key learning points
Delegation transfers a task, not accountability Give clear instructions and follow up
Address conflict with respect and evidence Use reflection to strengthen future practice

End-of-Program Summary By completing GNPS Program 9 - Level 1, you have developed the foundational knowledge required to practise accountably, apply ethical principles, protect patient rights and communicate professionally. These capabilities prepare you for Level 2 - International Qualified Nurse, where professional decisions are applied within different legal, cultural and regulatory systems.
